Abbo Floriacensis.bio: Monk and abbot of Fleury (Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire), educated at Paris and Reims. He spent 985–987 at Ramsey Abbey assisting Archbishop Oswald of York's monastic reforms, then returned to Fleury as abbot in 988, writing on computus, logic, canon law, and hagiography. He was killed at La Réole in Gascony in 1004, speared while trying to quell a fight between two factions of monks, and died in the arms of his disciple Aimoin, who later wrote his life.

Agobardus Lugdunensis.bio: Spanish-born archbishop of Lyon and one of the sharpest polemical minds of the Carolingian church. He wrote against judicial ordeals, against superstition about weather-magic, and on the relation of ecclesiastical to imperial authority, and took part in the revolts against Louis the Pious.

Alcuinus.bio: Northumbrian deacon, poet, and master of the cathedral school of York, whom Charlemagne drew to the Continent around 782 to lead the palace school at Aachen and direct the Carolingian revival of learning. He spent his last years as abbot of Saint-Martin of Tours. This compendious commentary on the Song of Songs is among his biblical works.

Anselmus Laudunensis.bio: Theologian and master of the cathedral school of Laon, whose teaching on the sacraments and on the ordered reading of Scripture shaped the twelfth-century schools. He and his circle are traditionally associated with the origins of the Glossa ordinaria on the Bible.

Auctor incertus._note: Generic label for works of uncertain authorship (Corpus Corporum / Migne 'Auctor incertus'). Renders as a plain 'Anonymous' byline with no popover; per-work provenance goes in work-about.json, not here, since this key is shared across many anonymous works.

Avitus Viennensis.bio: Bishop of Vienne in Burgundy, from a Gallo-Roman senatorial family, who worked to draw the Arian Burgundian kings toward Catholic Christianity. He left letters, homilies, and a biblical epic in verse on the events of Genesis and Exodus.

Guillelmus abbas.bio: Benedictine abbot of Saint-Thierry near Reims, who later laid down his abbacy to become a Cistercian monk at Signy; a close friend of Bernard of Clairvaux and the author of the first book of his life. He wrote his own exposition of the Song of Songs; the present work is an anthology he wove together from Bernard's sermons on the same book — hence 'ex Bernardo contexta,' compiled out of Bernard.

Haymo Halberstatensis.note: Migne prints this commentary under 'Haymo Halberstatensis' (Haimo, bishop of Halberstadt, d. 853). Much modern scholarship reassigns the Carolingian exegetical corpus printed under his name to Haimo of Auxerre; the attribution is unsettled — flagged for Wilson.

Hincmarus Rhemensis.bio: Archbishop of Reims for nearly forty years and the dominant ecclesiastical politician of the later Carolingian world. He wrote extensively on predestination, on royal and episcopal office, and on canon law, and shaped the practice of anointing West Frankish kings.

Hugo de S. Victore.bio: Theologian and head of the school of the abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, and the founding master of the Victorine tradition of learning and contemplation. His work ranges across the liberal arts (the Didascalicon), sacramental theology (De sacramentis christianae fidei), and mystical writing. The present piece is a short exposition of the Magnificat, the canticle of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Justus Urgellensis.bio: First bishop of Urgell in the Pyrenees (in present-day Catalonia), a signatory of the Second Council of Toledo (527) and the First Council of Lérida (546). His Explanatio in Cantica canticorum — which Migne prints as Explicatio — is dedicated to Sergius, archbishop of Tarragona, and is the earliest surviving Latin commentary on the Song of Songs.

Lanfrancus Cantuariensis.bio: Lombard jurist turned monk, prior of Bec and abbot of Caen before William the Conqueror made him archbishop of Canterbury. He argued the eucharistic case against Berengar of Tours and reorganised the English church, its councils, and its monastic observance.

Nicolaus Claraevallensis.bio: Monk of Montieramey and then of Clairvaux, where he served as secretary to Bernard until a breach of trust over the abbot’s seal ended his position there. His sermons and letters circulated widely, some of them long transmitted under Bernard’s name.

Odo Cameracensis.bio: Master of the cathedral school of Tournai, later abbot of the monastery he founded there and bishop of Cambrai. A realist logician and biblical expositor, he wrote on original sin and on the canon of the Mass, and ended his episcopate in exile over the investiture struggle.

Petrus Blesensis.bio: Letter-writer, poet and administrator, trained at Bologna and Paris, who served as secretary to the archbishops of Canterbury and archdeacon of Bath and London. His large and much-copied correspondence made him one of the most widely read prose stylists of the later twelfth century.

Petrus Damianus.bio: Hermit of Fonte Avellana, cardinal-bishop of Ostia, and the fiercest voice of the eleventh-century reform against simony and clerical marriage. His letters and short treatises are vehement, concrete, and often mordantly funny; Dante set him in the highest sphere of contemplatives.

Rabanus Maurus.bio: Pupil of Alcuin, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, and the most prolific compiler of the Carolingian renewal. His biblical commentaries and the encyclopaedic De rerum naturis transmitted patristic learning to the medieval schools; later ages called him praeceptor Germaniae.

Richardus S. Victoris.bio: Canon regular of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris — of British, probably Scottish, origin — and its prior from 1162. After Hugh, whose pupil he was, he was the leading theologian of the Victorine school: his De Trinitate reasoned toward the persons of God from the nature of perfect love, and his Benjamin minor and Benjamin major mapped the ascent to contemplation for generations of later readers.

Robertus Francorum.bio: King Robert II 'the Pious' of France (972–1031), the royal dedicatee of Abbo's Canones — not its author. Corpus Corporum lists him in the work's author array; he is filtered from author credit.

Robertus de Tumbalena.bio: Monk of Mont-Saint-Michel, later abbot of Saint-Vigor of Bayeux (1066–1084). He wrote this two-book commentary on the Song of Songs at the request of a fellow monk, Anastasius, prefacing it with a covering letter to a monk named Ansfrid.

Vincentius Lirinensis.bio: Monk of the island monastery of Lérins, off the coast of Provence, and one of the sharpest Latin minds of the semi-Pelagian milieu of southern Gaul. Around 434, three years after the Council of Ephesus, he composed the Commonitorium under the pen-name Peregrinus, 'the Pilgrim' — a handbook for telling catholic truth from heresy by the test of what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Migne prints the surviving first book together with the recapitulation that is all that remains of the lost second.

_README: Author display + modest bio, keyed by the exact Latin author-name string as it appears in a work's manifest.authors (and data/works.json). Populated incrementally as each author's first work ships — not a bulk backfill. Fields: displayName (English, used for bylines/crumbs/index; falls back to the Latin key when absent) · latin (the printed Latin form, shown in the author popup and carried in the index to disambiguate same-named authors) · dates · bio (modest, popup-length prose) · dedicatee (true = a royal/patron dedicatee Corpus Corporum lists in the author array but who did NOT write the work; filtered out of author credit). See translation-style.md and CLAUDE.md rule on English-first display.

Auctores varii._note: Generic label for composite pieces gathering texts by several hands (Corpus Corporum / Migne 'Auctores varii'). Renders as a plain byline with no popover; per-work provenance goes in work-about.json, not here, since this key is shared across many works.

Auctor incertus (Beda?).attributionFlag: Migne prints this among the Bedan dubia; the attribution to Bede is the edition's own conjecture and is not accepted by modern scholarship.
Auctor incertus (Beda?)._note: Shared anonymous key with a Bede attribution flag. No popover; per-work provenance goes in work-about.json.

Atto Vercellensis.bio: Lombard bishop of Vercelli from 924 until his death, and one of the more independent-minded canonists of tenth-century Italy. He served as grand chancellor to Hugh of Provence and to Lothar II as kings of Italy. His writings include the Polypticum, a bleak survey of the morals of his age; De pressuris ecclesiasticis, on the pressures brought to bear on ecclesiastical authority by lay power; and a Capitulare gathering the canon law of his province, drawing on the False Decretals and enlarged with provisions of his own.

Petrus diaconus.bio: Librarian and archivist of Monte Cassino, and for a time notary and secretary in the service of the emperor Lothar III. He continued the abbey chronicle begun by Leo Marsicanus and compiled its register of documents; he is also the most industrious forger of the twelfth century, and much of what he says about himself and his house was manufactured to defend its claims. His letters are read for their Senecan artistry as much as for their history.

Berno Augiae Divitis.bio: Abbot of Reichenau from 1008 until his death, and one of the leading liturgists and music theorists of his age. He wrote on the computus, on the chant and its tonary, and on the ordering of the church year — the last of which drew him into the exchange with Aribo of Mainz over how Advent is to be reckoned.

Auctor incertus (Augustinus Hipponensis?.attributionFlag: Migne prints these sermons among the pseudo-Augustiniana; the ascription to Augustine belongs to the manuscript rubrics, not to the text, whose orthography and idiom place it well after him.
Auctor incertus (Augustinus Hipponensis?._note: Shared anonymous key with an Augustinian attribution flag. No popover; per-work provenance goes in work-about.json.

Auctor incertus (Alcuinus?).attributionFlag: Migne gathers these pieces among Alcuin's dubia. The ascription holds for some of them — several name their author as Albinus, Alcuin's own byname — and is doubtful for others; the dossier is not the work of a single hand.
Auctor incertus (Alcuinus?)._note: Shared anonymous key with an Alcuinian attribution flag. No popover; per-work provenance goes in work-about.json.

Gualterus S. Victoris Parisiensis.bio: Canon regular of the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris, subprior under Richard and his successor as prior from 1173; his death is placed variously between 1179 and 1190. He is remembered almost entirely for the Contra quatuor labyrinthos Franciae, an unmeasured attack on Abelard, Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Lombard and Peter of Poitiers for handling the Trinity and the Incarnation with what he called scholastic levity. Some thirty of his sermons also survive.
Gualterus S. Victoris Parisiensis._note: Filed 2026-07-28, not yet a live byline target. Migne's own form, taken from the corpus rather than guessed: cc-pl-index authorIdno 2357, and the headnote in sources/pl/tei/11577.xml reads 'codex manuscriptus M. Gualteri de S. Victore' — NOT 'Galterus'. The death date is deliberately hedged: Catholic Encyclopedia c.1180, New Catholic Encyclopedia c.1190, Migne's own PL 199 headnote 'circa annum 1180'. He has one work in the corpus: idno 11577, Excerpta ex libris contra IV labyrinthos Franciae, PL 199 1129A-1172A, 17,454 words.

Joel.bio: 13th-century Byzantine chronicler; nothing is known of him beyond this work.
Joel._note: Migrated 2026-07-28 from pg-works.json authorNote, which no script read — Joel's PG page had no bio card at all. Keep bios HERE; pg-works.json is a queue register, not a display source.

Bruno Astensis.bio: Born at Solero in Piedmont and educated at Bologna, Bruno was made bishop of Segni in 1079 and consecrated by Gregory VII, whose reform he defended in print — his Libellus de simoniacis argues the case against simony. In 1099 he withdrew to Monte Cassino without giving up his see, and was elected its abbot in 1107; in 1111 Paschal II obliged him to resign the abbacy and return to Segni after he criticized the concessions of the Concordat of Ponte Mammolo. He died at Segni on 18 July 1123 and was canonized in 1181. His surviving work is overwhelmingly exegetical.

Auctor incertus (Cassiodorus Vivariensis._note: Shared anonymous key with a Cassiodorus attribution flag, following the Auctor incertus (Beda?) pattern. Per rule 8 no attribution research was opened; this records only what the edition itself shows.
